History:
- Chief complaint: New swelling of the left elbow noticed about 1 week ago.
- Symptoms: Swelling is not painful; area is slightly warm; sensation of some fluid inside; full elbow movement.
- Context: No recent injury or trauma reported; works at a desk; physically active with regular running.
- History of present illness: No prior similar episodes; no known acute injury; dry skin around the elbow.
- Medical history: Known osteoarthritis; peanut allergy; no regular medications.
- Family history: No documented rheumatologic diseases in family.

Past Medical History:
- Osteoarthritis (documented in the past; relation to current elbow swelling considered)
- Peanut allergy
- Regular exercise; otherwise healthy
- Allergies: peanuts

Physical Examination:
- Left elbow: Swelling present; the skin around the elbow slightly warm; dry skin noted at the tip of the elbow.
- Range of motion: Normal/ full.
- Tenderness: Not severely tender; pin-point tenderness at swelling area described as “weird” rather than intensely painful.
- No strong signs of septic arthritis observed during exam (no marked redness, systemic symptoms, or extreme pain noted).
- Other systems: Not recorded.

Impression:
- Primary: Suspected left olecranon bursitis (aseptic inflammatory bursitis) given localized swelling with mild warmth and preserved ROM.
- Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and investigation plan): 
  - Osteoarthritis with elbow effusion (history of OA; age 53; focal swelling)
  - Inflammatory/autoimmune arthritis (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthritis) – labs planned
  - Crystal arthropathy (gout or CPPD) – labs planned
  - Septic arthritis (considered but not supported by current exam; monitor for red flags)

Management Plan:
- Analgesia/anti-inflammatory: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally twice daily after meals; monitor for GI symptoms; discontinue if heartburn occurs.
- Diagnostic workup: Arrange blood tests to assess inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatologic antibodies; also screen for gout/CPPD. Blood test forms to be mailed with instructions; results expected in ~5–6 days.
- Follow-up: Schedule a follow-up appointment to review blood test results; options include in-person, telephone, or video visit.
- Red flags to monitor: If elbow becomes very red, very painful, or redness spreads rapidly or systemic symptoms develop, seek urgent evaluation.

Patient Summary:
- A middle-aged man with ~1 week of left elbow swelling, mild warmth, and preserved motion. Most likely olecranon bursitis; blood tests planned to assess inflammatory/infectious/autoimmune causes; ibuprofen started for symptom relief; follow-up planned after results.

Key Takeaways:
- Take ibuprofen with meals; stop if heartburn occurs.
- Complete the scheduled blood tests and follow up with results (telehealth or in-person).
- Seek urgent care if worsening redness, pain, swelling, or systemic symptoms develop.

Next Steps:
- Complete blood test collection and submission as instructed; await results in ~5–6 days.
- Attend follow-up (phone/video or in-clinic) to review blood tests and refine diagnosis and management.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: Vitals not recorded; comprehensive medication reconciliation not documented beyond current plan; exact allergen severity not detailed.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: Septic arthritis appears in the DDx but is explicitly considered unlikely by the clinician based on exam; no direct conflict in the documented plan, but acknowledged as a differential with low current likelihood.
- Transcript quality: Clear and coherent; sufficient detail to generate H&P.
